en: Majjhima Nikāya 114, the Discourse on What Should Be Cultivated and What Should Not Be Cultivated.
Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you a discourse on the Dhamma concerning what should be cultivated and what should not be cultivated.”
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Monks, I declare that bodily conduct is of two kinds:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated;
and these are mutually distinct forms of bodily conduct.”
“Monks, I declare that verbal conduct is of two kinds:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated;
and these are distinct from one another as verbal conduct.”
“Bhikkhus, I declare that mental conduct is twofold:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated—
and these two types of mental conduct are mutually distinct.”
“Monks, I say that even the arising of a state of mind is twofold:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated—
and these states of mind are mutually distinct.”
“Bhikkhus, I say that the acquisition of perception is of two kinds:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated—
and these acquisitions of perception are mutually distinct.”
“Monks, I declare that the acquisition of views is of two kinds:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated—
and these are mutually distinct acquisitions of views.”
“Monks, I say that the acquisition of an individual existence is of two kinds:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated;
and these are mutually distinct acquisitions of individual existence.”
When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Blessed One:
“Bhante, regarding this brief statement by the Blessed One whose meaning has not been analyzed in detail, I understand its meaning in detail as follows:
‘Monks, I say that bodily conduct is twofold—’”
“There is bodily conduct that should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated—
and these are mutually distinct,” so indeed was it said by the Blessed One.
And with reference to what was this said?
Venerable sir, whatever kind of bodily conduct one practices that causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to diminish—such bodily conduct should not be practiced.
But whatever kind of bodily conduct one practices that causes unwholesome states to diminish and wholesome states to increase—such bodily conduct should be practiced.
"Venerable sir, what kind of bodily conduct, when practiced, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline?
Here, venerable sir, a certain person is a destroyer of life—one who is cruel, with blood on his hands, intent on striking and killing, and devoid of compassion for living beings.
Furthermore, he is a taker of what is not given; he takes by way of theft what belongs to another, the property and belongings of others, whether found in a village or in the forest."

Furthermore, he engages in sexual misconduct; he has sexual relations with women who are protected by their mother, protected by their father, protected by both mother and father, protected by their brother, protected by their sister,
protected by their relatives, protected by their clan, protected by the Dhamma,
those who have a husband, those who are under threat of punishment, and even those who are merely betrothed with a flower garland— indeed, he has sexual relations with such women as these.
“Venerable sir, when one cultivates such bodily conduct, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline.
Venerable sir, when one cultivates what kind of bodily conduct do unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase?

Here, venerable sir, someone, having abandoned the destruction of life, abstains from the destruction of life; he lays aside the rod and the weapon, and dwells conscientious, compassionate, sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.”

Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; he does not take by way of theft what belongs to another, the property of another, whether it has gone into a village or a forest, if it is not given.

Having abandoned sexual misconduct, he abstains from sexual misconduct; he does not have sexual relations with women who are protected by their mother, protected by their father, protected by both parents, protected by their brother, protected by their sister, protected by their relatives, protected by their clan, or protected by the Dhamma.
He does not engage in improper conduct with women who have husbands and are under protection—even those protected by a mere garland of flowers.
Venerable sir, for one who cultivates such bodily conduct, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase.
“Monks, I declare that bodily conduct is of two kinds:”
"There is bodily conduct that should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated, and these are mutually distinct"—
this is what was said by the Blessed One, and it was said with reference to this.
“Monks, I declare that verbal conduct is of two kinds:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated—
and these are mutually distinct forms of verbal conduct.”
Thus indeed was it said by the Blessed One.
With reference to what was this said?
Venerable sir, whatever kind of verbal conduct one practices such that unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline—such verbal conduct should not be practiced.
"Venerable sir, such verbal conduct should be practiced that, by practicing it, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase.
But in what way, venerable sir, does unwholesome states increase and wholesome states diminish for one who practices such verbal conduct?
Here, venerable sir, a certain person is a speaker of falsehood. Whether in an assembly, in a gathering, or in the midst of his kinsmen..."
Or, having entered the midst of a crowd or having entered the royal court, being summoned and questioned as a witness:
"Come, good man, speak what you know," he says, "I know," when he does not know; or he says, "I do not know," when he knows; or he says, "I see," when he does not see;
or he says, "I do not see," when he sees—thus, for his own sake, or for the sake of another, or for the sake of some small material gain.
or speaks consciously what is false; moreover, he is one of malicious speech— he who, having heard something here, reports it there for the sake of dividing these people,
or having heard something there, reports it here for the sake of dividing those people— thus being a divider of those who are united, or a promoter of division among those who are divided.
He delights in factions, rejoices in factions, finds pleasure in factions, and speaks words that create factions.

Furthermore, he is harsh in speech; he speaks such words as are piercing, rough, harsh, bitter to others, offensive to others, bordering on anger, and conducive to lack of concentration. Moreover, he is a frivolous talker;

he speaks at the wrong time, speaks what is untrue, speaks what is useless, speaks according to non-Dhamma, and speaks according to non-discipline; he speaks words that are not worth treasuring—speaking at the wrong time, without foundation, indefinite, and unconnected with the goal.
"Venerable sir, for one who cultivates such verbal conduct, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline.
Venerable sir, for one who cultivates what kind of verbal conduct do unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase?
Here, venerable sir, someone, having abandoned false speech, abstains from false speech whether in an assembly or in a gathering."
Or, having been summoned as a witness and questioned in the midst of kinsmen, or in the midst of a guild, or in the midst of a royal court:
"Come, good man, speak what you know," he says, if he does not know: "I do not know," or if he knows:
"I know"; if he has not seen: "I have not seen," or if he has seen: "I have seen. Thus...
Whether for his own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of some trifling material gain, he does not speak falsehood with full awareness.
Having abandoned malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech:

having heard something here, he does not repeat it elsewhere for the purpose of dividing these people; nor, having heard something there, does he repeat it among these people for the purpose of dividing them. Thus, he does not cause division among those who are divided...

He is a reconciler of those who are divided or a provider of what is needed for those who are united; he delights in harmony, rejoices in harmony, finds joy in harmony, and speaks words that bring about harmony.

Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech; he speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, endearing, heart-reaching, urbane, agreeable to many people, and dear to many people.
Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks truthfully, speaks meaningfully, and speaks on what is beneficial.
One who speaks in accordance with the Dhamma, one who speaks in accordance with the Vinaya, is a speaker of speech that is well-founded, timely, reasoned, measured, and connected with the goal.
Venerable sir, for one who cultivates such verbal conduct, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase.
“Monks, I declare that verbal conduct is twofold:”
"There is verbal conduct that should be cultivated and verbal conduct that should not be cultivated— and these are distinct from one another"—
this is what was said by the Blessed One, and it was said with reference to this.
“Monks, I declare that mental conduct is of two kinds:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated;
and these are mutually distinct types of mental conduct.”
Thus indeed was it said by the Blessed One.
With reference to what was this said?
Venerable sir, whatever kind of mental conduct, when practiced, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to diminish—such mental conduct should not be practiced.
“Venerable sir, one should cultivate such mental conduct by following which unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase.
But in what way, venerable sir, does one who cultivates mental conduct cause unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to diminish?
Here, venerable sir, someone is covetous; he covets the wealth and property of others, thinking: ‘Oh, that what belongs to another were mine!’”
Furthermore, one has a mind full of ill will and a corrupt mental intention, thinking: “May these beings be slain, or executed, or cut off, or destroyed, or may they not even exist!
Venerable sir, for one who pursues such mental conduct, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline.
Venerable sir, by pursuing what kind of mental conduct do unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase?
“Here, venerable sir, a certain person is not covetous; he does not covet the wealth and possessions of others, thinking: ‘Oh, may what belongs to another be mine!

Furthermore, he has a mind free from ill will and intentions that are not corrupt, thinking: ‘May these beings be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from distress, and may they look after themselves with happiness.
Venerable sir, for one who cultivates such mental conduct, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase.”
“Monks, I declare that mental conduct is of two kinds:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated—
and these are mutually distinct forms of mental conduct.”
Thus, that which was said by the Blessed One was said with reference to this:
“Monks, I say that even the arising of a thought is twofold:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated.”
"And that [arises] from the mutual arising of consciousness"—
thus it was said by the Blessed One.
With reference to what was this said?
“Venerable sir, when one cultivates a certain kind of mental state, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline; such a mental state should not be cultivated.
But when one cultivates another kind of mental state, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase; such a mental state should be cultivated.
Venerable sir, what kind of mental state, when cultivated, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline?”
Here, venerable sir, a certain person is covetous; he dwells with a mind accompanied by covetousness;
he is ill-willed; he dwells with a mind accompanied by ill-will;
he is cruel; he dwells with a mind accompanied by cruelty.
“Venerable sir, when one cultivates such an arising of the mind, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline.
Venerable sir, when one cultivates what kind of arising of the mind do unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase?
Here, venerable sir, someone is not covetous; he dwells with a mind accompanied by non-covetousness.”
He is free from ill will and dwells with a mind accompanied by non-ill will;
he is free from cruelty and dwells with a mind accompanied by non-cruelty.
Venerable sir, for one who cultivates such an arising of the mind, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase.
“Bhikkhus, I say that even the arising of a state of mind is twofold:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated—
and these states of mind are mutually distinct.”
Thus, that which was said by the Blessed One was said with reference to this:
“Monks, I declare that the acquisition of perception is twofold:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated.”
"And that is the mutual attainment of perception"—
thus it was said by the Blessed One.
With reference to what was this said?
“Venerable sir, one should not cultivate that kind of attainment of perception by cultivating which unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline.
But, venerable sir, one should cultivate that kind of attainment of perception by cultivating which unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase.
Venerable sir, what kind of attainment of perception, when cultivated, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline?”
Here, venerable sir, a certain person is covetous; he dwells with perception accompanied by covetousness;
he is ill-willed; he dwells with perception accompanied by ill-will;
he is cruel; he dwells with perception accompanied by cruelty.
"Venerable sir, when one cultivates such an acquisition of perception, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline.
Venerable sir, when one cultivates what kind of acquisition of perception do unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase?
Here, venerable sir, someone is not covetous and dwells with a perception accompanied by non-covetousness."
He is free from ill will and dwells with a perception accompanied by non-ill will;
he is free from cruelty and dwells with a perception accompanied by non-cruelty.
Venerable sir, for one who cultivates such attainment of perception, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase.
“Monks, I say that the acquisition of perception is twofold:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated—
and these are mutually distinct acquisitions of perception.”
Thus, that which was said by the Blessed One was said with reference to this:
"Monks, I declare that the acquisition of views is of two kinds:
those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated."
"And that mutual acquisition of views"—
thus it was said by the Blessed One.
With reference to what was this said?
“Venerable sir, one should not cultivate a kind of acquisition of views such that, by cultivating it, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states diminish.
But, venerable sir, one should cultivate a kind of acquisition of views such that, by cultivating it, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase.
And what kind of acquisition of views, venerable sir, when cultivated, leads to the increase of unwholesome states and the diminution of wholesome states?”
"Here, venerable sir, a certain person holds such a view:
‘There is no giving, there is no offering, there is no sacrifice; there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done;
there is no this world, there is no other world; there is no mother, there is no father; there are no beings..."
‘There are no recluses or brahmins in the world who have attained the right path, who practice rightly, and who,
having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, make it known’— Venerable Sir,
when one cultivates such an acquisition of views, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline.
"Venerable sir, what kind of acquisition of view, when cultivated, causes unwholesome states to diminish and wholesome states to increase?
Here, venerable sir, a certain person holds such a view as this:
'There is what is given, there is what is sacrificed, there is what is offered; there is fruit and result of good and evil deeds.'"
‘There is kamma-result; there is this world; there is a world beyond; there is mother; there is father; there are beings who are spontaneously born;

there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who have fared rightly and practiced rightly, who have realized this world and the world beyond by their own direct knowledge and make it known to others’—thus one holds such a view.
“Venerable sir, for one who cultivates such an acquisition of views, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase.
‘Monks, I say that the acquisition of views is of two kinds:
that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.’”
And that acquisition of views is mutually [dependent]—
this is what was said by the Blessed One, and it was said with reference to this.
"Monks, I say that the acquisition of a personal existence is twofold."
"There is that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated;
and these are mutually related to the acquisition of individual existence"—
thus indeed was it said by the Blessed One.
And with reference to what was this said?
Venerable sir, whatever kind of acquisition of a personal existence, when pursued, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to diminish—
such an acquisition of a personal existence should not be pursued.
"Venerable sir, one should cultivate such an acquisition of individual existence that by cultivating it unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase. But in what way,
venerable sir, does one who cultivates an acquisition of individual existence cause unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to diminish?"
“Venerable sir, for one who produces a rebirth with a selfhood accompanied by affliction, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline because their state is not yet finalized.
Venerable sir, for one who produces a rebirth with a selfhood free from affliction, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase because their state is finalized.
‘Monks, I say that the acquisition of a selfhood is of two kinds:”
"There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated,
and these are mutually related to the acquisition of individual existence"—
this is what was said by the Blessed One, and it was said with reference to this.
“Venerable sir, regarding this brief statement spoken by the Blessed One, the meaning of which was not explained in detail, I understand its meaning in detail in this way.
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!
It is good, Sāriputta, that you understand the meaning in detail in this way of this brief statement spoken by me, the meaning of which was not explained in detail.”
“Monks, I say that bodily conduct is of two kinds:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated—
and these are distinct types of bodily conduct.”
Thus indeed was it said by me.
With reference to what was it said?
Sāriputta, whatever kind of bodily conduct, when practiced, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline—such bodily conduct should not be practiced.
But, Sāriputta, whatever kind of bodily conduct one practices such that unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase—
that kind of bodily conduct should be practiced.
And what kind of bodily conduct, Sāriputta, does one practice such that unwholesome states increase and wholesome states diminish?
"Here, Sāriputta, a certain person is a destroyer of life: he is cruel, bloody-handed, intent on killing and striking, and lacks compassion for living beings.
Furthermore, he is a taker of what is not given: whatever belongs to another, whether in a village or in the wilderness, he takes it by means of theft.
Moreover, he is one who engages in sexual misconduct: he has intercourse with women who are protected by their mother, protected by their father, or protected by both parents..."
One who engages in sexual misconduct with women protected by their mother, protected by their father, protected by their relatives, protected by their clan, protected by the Dhamma,
those who have a husband, those who are under threat of punishment, or even those who are merely surrounded by a circle of flowers—
by practicing such bodily conduct, Sāriputta, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline.
"In what way, Sāriputta, does unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase for one who cultivates a certain bodily conduct?

Here, Sāriputta, a certain person, having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from taking life; he lays aside the rod and the weapon, and dwells conscientious, full of compassion, sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.

Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; whatever belongs to another, whether in the village or in the forest, he does not take it by means of theft when it has not been given."

Having abandoned sexual misconduct, he abstains from sexual misconduct. He does not engage in sexual intercourse with those women who are protected by their mother, protected by their father, protected by both parents, protected by their brother, protected by their sister, protected by their relatives, protected by their clan, protected by Dhamma, or have a husband;
nor with those who are under legal protection, even down to those who are merely surrounded by a circle of flowers. In such cases, he does not commit an act of unchastity.
Sāriputta, for one who practices such bodily conduct, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase.
“Monks, I say that bodily conduct is of two kinds:
that which is to be practiced and that which is not to be practiced.”
"And that mutual bodily conduct"—this is what was said by me, and it was said with reference to this.
"And verbal conduct, monks, I declare to be twofold... [and so on].
“Monks, I declare that mental conduct is twofold...
I declare that the arising of thought is twofold...
I declare that the acquisition of perception is twofold...”
“Monks, I say that the acquisition of views is twofold … [as before] … Monks,
I say that the acquisition of individual existence is twofold:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated.”
"And that mutual acquisition of individual existence"—
thus indeed was this spoken by me.
With reference to what was this spoken?

Sāriputta, whatever kind of acquisition of individuality one cultivates such that unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, such an acquisition of individuality should not be cultivated.
But, Sāriputta, whatever kind of acquisition of individuality one cultivates such that unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase—
such an acquisition of individuality should be cultivated.
“Sāriputta, what kind of acquisition of a personal existence (attabhāvapaṭilābha), when cultivated, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to diminish?

Sāriputta, for one who produces an acquisition of a personal existence that is accompanied by affliction (sabyābajjha) and which does not lead to final completion, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states diminish.

Sāriputta, for one who produces an acquisition of a personal existence that is free from affliction (abyābajjha) and which leads to final completion, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase.”
“Bhikkhus, I say that the acquisition of a personal existence is of two kinds:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated;
and these are mutually distinct acquisitions of personal existence.”
Thus, that which was spoken by me, it was spoken with reference to this.
This, Sāriputta, is how the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief should be understood in detail:
"Sāriputta, I declare that form cognizable by the eye is twofold."
There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.
Sāriputta, I declare that even sound cognizable by the ear is of two kinds:
that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.
"Sāriputta, I declare that odors cognizable by the nose are of two kinds:
those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated.
Sāriputta, I declare that tastes cognizable by the tongue are of two kinds..."
There are things to be cultivated and things not to be cultivated.
Sāriputta, I declare that tactile objects cognizable by the body are of two kinds:
those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated.
“Sāriputta, I say that mental phenomena cognizable by the mind are of two kinds:
those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated.
When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Venerable sir, regarding this brief statement spoken by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not been analyzed in detail, I understand its meaning in detail as follows:
‘Sāriputta, I say that forms cognizable by the eye are of two kinds:
those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated.’”
Thus indeed was it said by the Blessed One.
With reference to what was this said?

Venerable sir, whatever kind of form cognizable by the eye that, when cultivated, increases unwholesome states and causes wholesome states to decline—such a form cognizable by the eye should not be cultivated.

"Venerable sir, whatever kind of form cognizable by the eye, when cultivated, causes unwholesome states to diminish and wholesome states to increase—that kind of form cognizable by the eye should be cultivated.
'Sāriputta, I say that form cognizable by the eye is of two kinds:
that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.'"
Thus, that which was said by the Blessed One was said with reference to this:
“Sāriputta, regarding sound cognizable by the ear...
such a sound cognizable by the ear should not be cultivated... [and so on].
Such a sound cognizable by the ear should be cultivated;
such an odor cognizable by the nose should not be cultivated;
such an odor cognizable by the nose should be cultivated.
Such a taste cognizable by the tongue should not be indulged in… such a taste cognizable by the tongue may be indulged in… And as for a tactile object cognizable by the body, Sāriputta…
“Such a tangible object cognizable by the body should not be cultivated...
such a tangible object cognizable by the body should be cultivated.
‘Sāriputta, I say that a mental phenomenon cognizable by the mind is of two kinds:”
‘There are things to be cultivated and things not to be cultivated’—
thus it was said by the Blessed One.
With reference to what was this said?

“Venerable sir, whatever kind of mental object cognizable by the mind that, when cultivated, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline—such a mental object cognizable by the mind should not be cultivated.

And whatever kind of mental object cognizable by the mind that, when cultivated, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase—such a mental object cognizable by the mind should be cultivated.
‘I say, Sāriputta, that a mental object cognizable by the mind is of two kinds—”
‘There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated’—
this is what was said by the Blessed One, and it was said with reference to this.
Venerable sir, this is how I understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief by the Blessed One, the meaning of which had not been analyzed.”
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!
It is good that you, Sāriputta, understand in such detail the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief and not yet analyzed in detail:
‘Sāriputta, I say that form cognizable by the eye is twofold:’”
‘There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated’—
thus indeed was this said by me.
With reference to what was this said?
"Sāriputta, when one cultivates a kind of form cognizable by the eye such that unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, such a form cognizable by the eye should not be cultivated.
But, Sāriputta, when one cultivates a kind of form cognizable by the eye such that unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase, such a form cognizable by the eye should be cultivated.
'Sāriputta, I say that form cognizable by the eye is of two kinds: [the kind to be cultivated and the kind not to be cultivated.]'"
‘There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated’—this is what I have said, and it was in reference to this that I spoke.
Sariputta, regarding sound cognizable by the ear... [and so on].
Such a sound cognizable by the ear should not be cultivated...
such a sound cognizable by the ear should be cultivated...
such an odor cognizable by the nose should not be cultivated...
Such a scent cognizable by the nose should be cultivated;
such a taste cognizable by the tongue should not be cultivated;
such a taste cognizable by the tongue should be cultivated.
"Such a tangible object cognizable by the body should not be cultivated...
such a tangible object cognizable by the body should be cultivated.
And as for a mental phenomenon cognizable by the mind, Sāriputta... [and so on]."
“Such a mental object cognizable by the mind should not be cultivated… such a mental object cognizable by the mind should be cultivated.
‘Sāriputta, I declare that a mental object cognizable by the mind is of two kinds— ”
‘There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated’—
this is what was said by me, and it was said with reference to this.
Sāriputta, the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief should be understood in detail in this way.
“Sāriputta, I say that robes are of two kinds:
those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated...
Likewise, Sāriputta, I say that almsfood is of two kinds...”
“Sāriputta, I have said that a lodging is [a condition for the arising of unarisen taints and for the increase of arisen taints]… a village, Sāriputta… a town, Sāriputta…”
"Sāriputta, I speak of a city in two ways;
Sāriputta, I speak of a country in two ways;
Sāriputta, I speak of a person in two ways."
“...that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.
When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, regarding this brief statement by the Blessed One whose meaning has not been analyzed in detail, I understand its meaning in detail as follows.”
“‘I say, Sāriputta, that robes are of two kinds:
those to be used and those not to be used’—
thus indeed was it said by the Blessed One.”
On what account was this said?
Venerable sir, whatever kind of robe one uses that causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline—such a robe should not be used.
But whatever kind of robe one uses that causes unwholesome states to decline and wholesome states to increase—such a robe should be used.
“‘I say, Sāriputta, that robes are of two kinds:
those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated’—
this is what was said by the Blessed One, and it was said with reference to this.”
“Almsfood, Sāriputta, I say … [as above] … such almsfood should not be consumed;
such almsfood should be consumed.”
“Sāriputta, as for lodgings... [as before] ... such a lodging should not be frequented;
such a lodging should be frequented.”
“Sāriputta, I say that such a village should not be frequented … [as before] … such a village should be frequented.”
A market town of such a kind should not be frequented… a market town of such a kind may be frequented… a city of such a kind should not be frequented…
A city such as this should be frequented… a country such as this should not be frequented… a country such as this should be frequented.
“‘I say, Sāriputta, that a person is of two kinds:
one who is to be associated with and one who is not to be associated with’—
thus indeed was it said by the Blessed One.”
And with reference to what was this said?
Venerable sir, one should not associate with such a person as, by associating with whom, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline.
But, venerable sir, one should associate with such a person as, by associating with whom, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase.
“‘I say, Sāriputta, that there are two kinds of persons:
those who are to be associated with and those who are not to be associated with’—
this is what was said by the Blessed One, and it was said in reference to this.”
“Bhante, regarding this which was spoken by the Blessed One in brief and whose meaning has not been analyzed in detail, this is how I understand its meaning in detail.
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!
It is well that you, Sāriputta, understand in such detail the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief and whose meaning had not been analyzed in detail.”
“‘I say, Sāriputta, that robes are of two kinds:
those to be used and those not to be used’—
thus indeed was it said by me.”
And with reference to what was this said?
Sāriputta, whatever kind of robe, when used, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline—such a robe should not be used.
But whatever kind of robe, Sāriputta, when used, causes unwholesome states to decline and wholesome states to increase—such a robe should be used.
“‘I say, Sāriputta, that robes are of two kinds:
those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated.
This is what was said by me, and it was said with reference to this.”
(As in the first [case], so it should be expanded in detail:
Such almsfood...
such a lodging...
Such a village...
such a market town...
such a city...
“Such is the kind of country.
‘I say, Sāriputta, that there are two kinds of persons:
those who should be associated with and those who should not be associated with.’”
Thus indeed was this spoken by me.
With reference to what was it said?
Sāriputta, when by associating with a certain kind of person unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, such a person should not be associated with.
"Sāriputta, one should associate with a person such that, by associating with them, unwholesome qualities diminish and wholesome qualities increase.
'Sāriputta, I say that there are two kinds of persons:
those to be associated with and those not to be associated with.'"
Thus, that which was spoken by me has been spoken with reference to this.
This, Sāriputta, is how the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief should be understood in detail.

If all the khattiyas, Sāriputta, were to understand the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief in such a detailed way, it would lead to the welfare and happiness of those khattiyas for a long time.
If all the brahmins, Sāriputta— and likewise all the vessas,
and all the suddas— were to understand the detailed meaning of what I have spoken in brief in this way, it would lead to the welfare and happiness of all those suddas for a long time.
“Sāriputta, if the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans,
were to understand the detailed meaning of this brief statement as I have spoken it,
that would lead to the welfare and happiness of this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, of this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, for a long time.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Sāriputta, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The fourth discourse, “The Discourse on What Should Be Cultivated and What Should Not Be Cultivated,” is finished.
